text:
For on-device storage, adopt a local relational database like SQLite combined with a CRDT-based text engine (such as Yjs or Automerge) for the note content, while storing attachments in the file system. Reject NoSQL solutions like Realm or WatermelonDB because they add complex sync-layer dependencies that are overkill for an offline-first start and difficult to manage without a server. SQLite is mature, widely supported on both iOS and Android, and requires zero external dependencies. Use Yjs or Automerge embedded directly into the app code rather than relying on external sync servers. This choice ensures data portability; since the storage format is JSON-like (for text) and standard files (for attachments), it can be easily ingested by any future backend without proprietary lock-in. The rejection of server-dependent architectures is critical because the first release has no network capability, and switching engines later would require a painful data migration, violating the constraint of seamless transition.

To handle concurrent edits without losing text, implement Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) using Yjs or Automerge. These libraries use operational transformation logic internally to merge changes from two devices automatically based on character indices rather than whole-document overwrites. When Developer A edits the first paragraph and Developer B edits the third paragraph simultaneously, the CRDT engine merges both changes into a single coherent document state upon the next sync. Reject manual 'last-write-wins' strategies or database-level locks because they inevitably lead to data loss for one user’s work, which violates the user expectation of not losing text. The key technical advantage here is that CRDTs guarantee eventual consistency without requiring a central authority to arbitrate versions, making them ideal for a peer-to-peer sync model that may later transition to a client-server model.

When a true conflict occurs—such as both users deleting the same block of text or editing overlapping characters differently—the system must surface the ambiguity to the user. Instead of silently dropping changes, generate two separate versions of the note locally: the 'local' version and the 'remote' version. In your UI, display a unified diff view or a side-by-side comparison tool. Allow the user to manually merge the desired text back into the primary note. This approach preserves all data while acknowledging the conflict. Reject automated resolution for semantic conflicts (like overlapping edits) because CRDTs handle disjoint edits automatically; manual intervention is only needed for true collisions where both users modified the same span. For attachments, use checksum-based deduplication. If two devices upload the same 10MB file, the sync service (when implemented) or local storage should recognize the hash match and store it only once, preventing bloat in the future hosted storage.

The migration path from 'no server' to a 'hosted sync service' relies on maintaining a dual-sync architecture from day one. Even without a server, implement a local-to-local sync protocol (like Bluetooth or Wi-Fi Direct for proximity) that uses the same CRDT state vectors used for cloud sync. Structure your data model with two 'roots': one for local-only storage and one for cloud sync. Initially, the cloud root is empty or dormant. When you launch the hosted service, it simply begins writing to this pre-existing cloud root structure. Existing users’ data resides in the local root; when they connect to the new service, their device uploads its CRDT state vectors to the server. The server acts as a neutral broker, not altering the data but providing the missing state to other devices. This means no user migration script is needed because the database schema remains identical. The only change is the addition of an API endpoint that accepts and returns the same JSON/CRDT payloads your local app already understands.

To ensure this works seamlessly for existing users, implement a 'sync adapter' pattern in your codebase. This interface abstracts the data transport mechanism. Initially, the adapter points to a local file or Bluetooth listener. When you launch the service, you swap the adapter implementation to an HTTP client pointing to your new backend. Since the payload format (CRDT state) is unchanged, existing notes sync automatically when devices come online. Reject the idea of forcing a manual export/import process because it breaks the 'offline-first' trust; users expect their data to be safe locally. By keeping the local store immutable and adding the cloud layer as a transparent overlay, you preserve user trust and avoid migration friction. The hosted service essentially becomes just another peer in the sync network, which simplifies testing and deployment.

The primary risks of this architecture are performance degradation on mobile devices due to large CRDT state sizes and the complexity of implementing conflict resolution UIs. As notes grow or are edited frequently, CRDT metadata can bloat, slowing down sync calculations on low-end phones. Another risk is the 'split-brain' scenario where no server exists to provide a single source of truth during prolonged outages, leading to divergent histories that are hard to reconcile later. To find these risks early, conduct stress tests with simulated network partitions and large datasets. Measure CRDT state size growth over 1,000 edits per note; if state exceeds 50KB, consider implementing 'structural sharing' or periodic compaction strategies to prune old operations. Monitor sync latency during offline periods by forcing devices to generate massive concurrent edits manually.

Early validation of the conflict resolution UX is critical. Build a prototype where two simulated instances of the app run on the same device but with separate memory spaces, and force overlapping edits. Observe if users can intuitively resolve the diff view within 30 seconds. If they struggle, simplify the UI by prioritizing text diffs over attachment handling in the conflict view. Additionally, test the migration path early by creating a local-only database, then writing a script that injects a 'cloud root' and simulates an upload. Verify that existing notes remain intact and that new sync events propagate correctly without corrupting the original data structure. This proactive testing ensures that when you launch the service, the transition is invisible to users, preserving your zero-migration constraint.

Finally, define success metrics for the no-server phase: ensure that 100% of edits persist locally regardless of network state, and that concurrent edits on two devices merge correctly without data loss. Track the frequency of conflicts to assess if CRDTs are handling most cases automatically or if manual resolution is becoming a bottleneck. If manual conflicts exceed 10% of syncs, re-evaluate your edit granularity or UI design. By focusing on these metrics, you ensure that the core value proposition—reliable, offline-first storage with non-destructive syncing—is robust before investing in backend infrastructure. This disciplined approach allows two developers to ship a stable product while laying a foundation for scalable, server-driven sync that respects user data integrity and ease of migration.
